newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: YEAREND - Insurers read warning signs in Asia.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND - Insurers read warning signs in Asia.

text.p: Asia appears the stuff of dreams for Western insurers hopeful of double-digit premium growth, but every silver lining has a cloud, as Swiss Reinsurance Co's research bulletin showed in October.
The report, called Sigma, predicted real annual premium growth in Asia at above 10 percent to the year 2000. The global average is four percent.
But Sigma warned that "anticipated profit gains could fail to materialise if large international capacities are brought to bear on the still rather modest demand volume".
Players are already concerned about over-capacity among the 850 or so insurers underwriting in Asia.
In Singapore, the market's regional hub, the slowdown has arrived.
Premium growth in 1995 was 11 percent, down from the 1991 high of 19.4 percent. And the most optimistic in the industry have predicted only moderate expansion in coming years.

Most growth will come from the life business, particularly when the island republic's state pension programme rules are relaxed in 1997. The general sector, in which foreign business actually shrank 3.4 percent in 1995, will be tied to the overall economy, which is also slowing.

In Hong Kong, a sluggish economy and an over-crowded market are expected to bring flat growth of about two percent for general insurers in 1996, the same as in 1995, but well short of the 16 percent of 1994.
Meanwhile, insurers await a government review of claims reserves, which ratings agency Standard & Poor's Corp has said could be a shortfall of Hong Kong $2 billion ($258.4 million).

Japan has already fallen behind in the Asian insurance growth rate stakes, according to Sigma. But the recently concluded insurance liberalisation deal with the United States is expected to intensify competition in a market seen as the region's most developed and worth about $400 billion.
In Australia, low claims volumes and abundant capacity have impacted on rates, said Tony Jackson, insurance analyst with stockbroker Macquarie Equities.

But he said the industry showed underlying health, helped by factors such as the Australian $200 million ($158 million) stock exchange debut in December of New Cap Reinsurance Corp Holdings Ltd, the demutualisation of large life insurance players and the privatisation of government-backed insurers.
Australian Mutual Provident Society (AMP), the country's largest life company, is expected to demutualise in early 1997.
In Thailand, growth is also expected to slow next year.
Industry sources said premium growth in 1996 had dropped to about 10 percent from the 30 percent of recent years.
Saravoot Phasuvanichphongse, president of the Thai General Insurance Association, told Reuters higher claims, low economic growth and plans to issue new licences would impact company results.
"If the government grants many more licences, it will substantially affect existing companies," said Saravoot.

The licences due are the first new licences in 14 years and 66 foreign firms met the entry criteria in January. None has yet received a licence to join the existing 62-company market and a change of government since has not clarified the matter.

Philippine insurance commissioner Eduardo Malinis expects general insurance premiums to rise 11.1 percent to 21 billion pesos ($798.5 million) in 1997, less than the 12.8 percent rise to 18.9 billion pesos estimated for 1996.
Most foreign interest in the Philippines, open to overseas entrants since 1992, has been in life business -- where four new licences have been granted -- and reinsurance.
No foreign non-life primary insurance player has set up, largely because of the country's exposure to natural disasters.
Restructuring has gathered pace in Malaysia, where insurance authority Bank Negara has said it wants 15 to 20 well-capitalised insurers to be able to compete in the open market by 2000.
Industry watchers think this would involve Bank Negara prompting some units in the 60-company market to merge.

The latest Bank Negara figures show premiums rose 17.8 percent in 1995 to 4.6 billion ringgit ($1.8 billion) with general insurers turning in an underwriting profit of 479 million ringgit in 1995 against 290 million ringgit in 1994.

Pakistan's insurance market has continued to exhibit optimism, despite a bad year for law and order which had an adverse impact on motor and burglary insurance results, EFU General Insurance Ltd chief executive Saifuddin Zoomkawala, said.
Mohamed Hanif Adamjee, chairman of Adamjee Insurance Company Ltd, said: "In spite of the difficult conditions through which we are passing, our outlook is optimistic."

Vietnam's fledgling market has shown positive signs. Premium growth has been estimated to be about 40 percent in 1996, roughly the same level as the past two years, although it would come from a low base of $150 million.

While market liberalisation began in 1994, domestic insurer Bao Viet still has about an 80 percent share. Only one foreign joint venture has been created, led by Bao Viet with partners Commercial Union Plc and Tokio Fire and Marine Insurance Company A second, linking state-run Bao Minh, Yasuda Fire & Marine Insurance Co Ltd and Mitsui Marine & Fire Insurance Co Ltd, is expected soon.

The life business got off the ground only in 1996 and has been hampered by the lack of a treasury investment and stock market, which would aid long term investment positions. But the coming of a stock market is on the horizon, said Dudley Bates, group representative of Guardian Insurance in Hanoi.
In China, officials have resisted admitting too many foreign firms.
Peter Spalti, chairman of Winterthur Swiss Insurance Co, the first European insurer to write a non-life book in China, said he sympathised with their concerns.
"They don't want surprises. There are many reasons for doing things this way (gradually)," he said.
But the rapid growth forecast for China, with premiums predicted to hit 200-250 billion yuan ($24-$30 billion) by 2000 from 1995's 61.6 billion yuan, is a huge draw.
(US$1 = yuan 8.30)
(US$1 = peso 26.30
(US$1 = ringgit 2.52)
